Subantarctic fur seal pups are born during the austral summer on remote islands such as Amsterdam Island and Île de la Possession. Neonates enter the world with a mean wet weight at birth of 4220 grams [Wwb = 4220 grams], a substantial mass that supports thermoregulation in the cool marine environment. Observations of lactating females on Macquarie Island indicate that the maximum reproductive rate under optimal foraging conditions corresponds to one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] and one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] at the typical core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This rate, representing the highest possible annual output, is constrained by the energetic demands of a long lactation period and the need to rebuild maternal reserves between breeding seasons. The timing of parturition is tightly synchronized with local productivity cycles, ensuring that neonatal emergence coincides with peak prey availability for the mother. Field studies using repeated resightings of tagged females have confirmed that virtually all sexually mature adults produce a single offspring annually, with twinning being exceptionally rare in this species and typically associated with poor pup survival. The link between maternal body condition and reproductive success is well documented, with heavier females exhibiting higher weaning rates for their pups.

The gestation period in Subantarctic fur seals includes a lengthy period of embryonic diapause, a reproductive strategy common among otariids. Accounting for both the delayed implantation and the active foetal development stage, total gestation time is 257 days [tg = 257 days] at a maternal core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This interval begins with copulation and ends with parturition, though the embryo remains in a quiescent state for several months before implantation occurs. The active foetal growth phase itself is relatively brief, lasting roughly four months, during which the developing foetus undergoes organogenesis and rapid mass accretion. Comparative data from the closely related South American fur seal (Arctocephalus australis) indicate that the maximum lifespan recorded is 30.6 years [am = 30.6 years] at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a figure that likely applies to Subantarctic fur seals given their similar life history pace. This longevity is modest compared to some phocid seals but typical for otariids, reflecting the trade-off between reproductive effort and somatic maintenance over a multi-decadal lifespan.

Maternal investment extends well beyond parturition, as pups rely entirely on milk for their initial months. The time since birth at weaning is 239 days [tx = 239 days] under standard maternal core temperature conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lengthy nursing period is among the longest recorded in otariids and reflects the dilute, high-fat composition of the milk, which supports gradual but sustained mass gain. During this interval, pups increase their body mass more than fivefold while developing the diving and foraging skills necessary for independent survival. Weaning itself is an abrupt event, triggered by the mother's departure from the colony after her final nursing bout. Post-weaning, juveniles face a critical period of nutritional independence during which they must locate productive foraging grounds without maternal guidance. Mortality rates during the first year after weaning can be substantial, particularly for individuals born late in the breeding season or to primiparous mothers, highlighting the importance of the extended pre-weaning developmental phase.

Sexual maturation in females follows a different trajectory than in males, reflecting divergent reproductive strategies. Females reach puberty at 3.5 years after birth [tp = 3.5 years after birth] at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a relatively early age that allows them to begin contributing to the breeding population while still completing somatic growth. Males, by contrast, attain sexual maturity at 5 years after birth [tp = 5 years after birth] under the same thermal regime of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This delayed maturation in males is attributed to the intense intrasexual competition for territories and access to females, which requires a large body size and substantial energy reserves. Subadult males exhibit gradual increases in testicular volume and circulating androgen levels, with full reproductive competency not achieved until they can successfully defend a breeding territory among older, more experienced bulls. The divergence in pubertal timing between the sexes is a common pattern in polygynous pinnipeds, where variance in reproductive success is far higher among males.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, a hallmark of its polygynous mating system. This threefold difference in mass reflects strong sexual selection for male fighting ability and territory acquisition during the breeding season. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 50,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 50,000 grams], a mass that supports their energetic demands of gestation and lactation, while males attain a much larger ultimate wet weight of 160,000 grams [Wwi = 160,000 grams], enabling them to compete successfully for access to females. The reproductive frequency is one pupping event per year [Ri = one pupping event per year], with each event yielding a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter]. Energetic modeling based on doubly labeled water studies suggests that lactating females must increase their food intake by roughly 70 percent above maintenance levels to sustain milk production. The cost of lactation is particularly high in this species because pups remain dependent for such an extended period, requiring mothers to alternate between foraging trips at sea and nursing bouts on land throughout the austral summer and early autumn.
